Early- versus Late-Decision Accounts of the Readiness Potential (RP)/the Stochastic Accumulator Model

(A) Early-decision accounts of the RP propose that the onset of the RP marks an inflection point in neural activity, the start of a process of planning and preparation for movement that culminates in a movement at _t_0\. According to early-decision accounts, the neural decision to initiate movement is marked by the onset of the RP. (B) In late-decision accounts, the RP reflects the average time course of ongoing spontaneous fluctuations in neural firing rate, recruitment, or excitability when data are time-locked to crests in those fluctuations. The accumulation-to-bound model (AtBM; C–F) offers a late-decision account of the RP. The AtBM accounts for the RP using a leaky stochastic accumulator. The distribution of first crossing times (blue arrows in C) can be used to account for the distribution of waiting times in Libet’s \[[2](#R2)\] task (E). When the decision variable is time-locked to the threshold crossing (D), its average trajectory (sign reversed) as it approaches the threshold can be fit to the shape of the RP (F).

### Box 4\. The Accumulation-to-Bound Model.

The AtBM posits that the RP reflects ongoing stochastic fluctuations in neural activity that play a role in fixing the precise time of movement onset when timing is relatively unconstrained \[[41](#R41)\]. When there are no external inputs to that decision, such as in the Libet task, the question ‘do I move now, or later?’ has to be resolved somehow. The ongoing temporally autocorrelated stochastic ebb and flow of brain activity could be one factor. If ongoing fluctuations can tip the scales in favor of moving now, then time-locking to movement onset becomes equivalent to time-locking to crests in the underlying autocorrelated neural time series. The time-locked average will then, at least in part, reflect the random buildup to those crests (see [Figure 1](#F1) in main text). While this may not explain the peak of the RP, which probably originates in the primary motor cortex, it can explain the early phase of the RP. The AtBM is a ‘late decision’ account in that the threshold crossing event that leads to movement is proximal to the movement and late in the evolution of the classic RP. The RP onset (deviation from baseline) on this model is physiologically meaningless: it does not mark a causally efficacious neural event or process.

The underlying process is modeled using a leaky stochastic accumulator, a kind of AtBM (or accumulator to bound model). Such models have been used for decades to model various kinds of cued decision-making tasks \[[113](#R113)–[116](#R116)\] and have also been used to account for decision-related neural activity, notably in posterior parietal cortex, in perceptual decision-making tasks \[[117](#R117)–[119](#R119)\]. The accumulator process is given by 

| dx\=(I−kx)dt+cξdt | \[I\] |
| ----------------- | ----- |

and has three free parameters: an imperative signal _I_, a leak current _k_, and a threshold on _x_ (which is called the decision variable). On average, the decision variable will climb to a mean value of _I/k_ and then fluctuate randomly around that mean value, eventually reaching an appropriately chosen threshold. The average trajectory of the decision variable as it approaches the threshold can be fit to electrophysiological data, such as the RP, and the distribution of first threshold-crossing times can be fit to the empirical distribution of waiting times in a self-initiated movement task \[[41](#R41)\]. More recently it has also been shown that, under certain assumptions, the average input to the accumulator also has a ramping character that can fit the RP \[[43](#R43)\].

While late-decision accounts of the RP may be less intuitive than the goal-directed interpretation offered by the classical early-decision account, they are, arguably, more parsimonious. Why should there be such a long and highly variable lag, of up to one second or more, between the decision to initiate movement and movement onset? Why has the RP not proven to be a very reliable real-time predictor of movement onset? And why are subjective reports of the (conscious) decision time so late relative to the supposed ‘onset’ of the RP? These puzzling questions are not at all puzzling from a late-decision perspective, so the onus should be on proponents of the early-decision account to explain why the more parsimonious late-decision view is false.

Recent physiological evidence embraces the decision-to-bound framework and corroborates the late-decision interpretation. Neurophysiological work in rats \[[44](#R44)\] found that ramping activity in the rat secondary motor cortex (M2) could be explained similarly. This ramping activity preceded spontaneous decisions to abandon waiting for a large reward and instead opt for a small but certain reward. The authors were able to account for this ramping activity using a leaky **stochastic accumulator model**, the same model used by \[[41](#R41)\] to capture the RP profile in human EEG. Subsequent work found that the buildup’s stochastic component was reflected by activity in area M2, but not medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), which instead accounted for deterministic biases in action timing \[[45](#R45)\]. This suggests a two-stage model of the RP in which a signal that can lead to movement only does so when it coincides in time with a stochastic fluctuation that then pushes the system over the threshold for movement.

Consistent with the stochastic account, some neuroscientists \[[46](#R46)\] propose that the RP reflects a tendency for movement initiation to coincide with negative-going fluctuations in the EEG slow-cortical potential (_cf_. \[[47](#R47)\]). They call this idea the selective slow-cortical-potential (SCP) sampling hypothesis. Like the AtBM, the SCP sampling hypothesis rests on the premise that there are ongoing (presumably stochastic) slow fluctuations in cortical potential. Furthermore, the motor system is somewhat more excitable during the negative phases of these fluctuations, making spontaneous voluntary movement more likely at those times. Like all SDMs, this account raises the same challenge to the classic interpretation: the RP does not reflect a process of ‘planning and preparation for movement’ and cannot be used to argue against the existence of conscious volition.

Other variants of the stochastic account are possible. One posits that subjects periodically rehearse the movement they were instructed to make and that these subthreshold rehearsal events interact with ongoing fluctuations in the motor system. When the sum of the ongoing fluctuations and the motor-rehearsal events crosses the threshold, the movement is initiated. This sum will also produce a slow buildup in the average time-locked to movement onset. Another possibility is that motivational signals produce brief subthreshold motor impulses at random times, which are integrated downstream. A leaky integral over this input would reflect the temporal density of the impulses, which would lead to movement onset when it reaches a threshold. While these alternatives may have slightly different philosophical implications, they are notably similar to the late-decision accumulator model.

Since the introduction of the AtBM \[[41](#R41)\] a few studies have challenged the late-decision view, or bolstered the early-decision view. One \[[48](#R48)\] looked at across-trial variance in the RP as a function of time (see \[[31](#R31)\]) and found that variance decreased at a greater rate before self-initiated movements than cued movements. This could be accounted for by incorporating a reduction in noise over time, before self-initiated actions, into the same stochastic accumulator model used by Schurger _et al_. \[[41](#R41)\]. While this decrease in variance over time leading up to movement onset may seem to be a compelling sign that the motor system is preparing a movement, it is no more compelling than the profile of the RP itself, which had seemed like incontrovertible evidence of preparation until the SDM provided an alternative, arguably more compelling, interpretation. A change in some variable (whether the mean or variance) in advance of an event, however compelling it may seem, does not entail a process of intentional preparation for that event \[[42](#R42)\]. Future studies may clarify these issues.

According to the AtBM, the RP appears in the movement-locked average because the onset of self-initiated movement tends to coincide in time with crests in ongoing stochastic fluctuations in neuronal activity. If true, then deflections, perhaps resembling the RP, approaching but not crossing the movement threshold, should happen regularly even when the subject is not making any movements. In one study \[[49](#R49)\], the (averaged) RP was used as a filter to search for RP-like events in EEG data from subjects performing a self-initiated movement task. Because the noise in an EEG recording is an order of magnitude greater in amplitude than the signal and because that noise is temporally autocorrelated, any such filter applied to single-trial EEG data will uncover RP-like events. But these turn out to be unrelated to the weaker, hidden deflections that give rise to the RP in the movement-locked average. Therefore, further research is required, ideally with invasive recordings, to determine whether or not RP-like events happen all the time.

Whether a late- or early-decision account more aptly accounts for the data remains an open question, but, as mentioned previously, the late-decision position has parsimony on its side. Also, other evidence points to a decisive event within the last 200 ms before movement onset, consistent with the late-decision account. There is an abrupt increase in corticospinal excitability in the last 100 ms before muscle contraction (\~150 ms before movement), but no changes in corticospinal excitability prior to that \[[50](#R50)\]. More recently, a study that used a clever paradigm involving a BCI \[[13](#R13)\] estimated the time of the **point-of-no-return** in self-initiated movement to be about 200 ms before movement onset (cf. \[[51](#R51)\]). Finally, Libet \[[2](#R2)\] and many replications since then have found that, when asked when they had (consciously) decided to move, subjects reliably and consistently point to about 150–200 ms before movement onset. According to the classic early-decision account of the RP, this must mean that the brain was already preparing to move long before awareness of a decision to move. But according to the late-decision account, it is simply a sign that, when asked to report the time at which a decisive neural event took place, subjects are reasonably accurate in doing so.

## Relevance of the RP for Discussions of Free Will

The notion that neuroscience could demonstrate the inefficacy of conscious will naturally captured much attention from philosophers and psychologists and it remains an active subject of debate \[[52](#R52)\]. The arguments for the inefficacy of conscious will rely upon the following three associated implicit commitments. First, that the RP itself is postdecisional: it occurs after the decision to move. Second, that the RP is ontologically real: it reflects an identifiable, causally efficacious process that begins at RP onset and culminates in movement. Third, since the signal reflects a real process, it is natural to assume that the onset of the RP marks a significant moment at which the process leading to movement begins.

SDMs provide a compelling alternative. Underlying SDMs is the idea that ordinary decision processes give rise to the decision to move. This seems almost tautological, but it is revolutionary for the interpretation of the RP. Standard accumulation-to-bound mechanisms, when time-locked to movement and averaged, and when the ‘evidence’ is weak relative to the noise, necessarily produce a trace that has the profile of the RP. The decision to move occurs when the threshold is reached prior to movement and the ‘onset’ of the RP does not correspond to a meaningful event: it is just an artifact of the averaging process. In any individual trial that leads to movement, it may not be possible to identify a point at which the process began since the excursion to threshold may not be monotonic. Furthermore, since the ‘onset’ of the RP does not correspond to a physiologically real event in individual trials, it is senseless to consider the relationship of the time of that (non)event to any other, such as W-time. In other words, the stochastic model accounts for all the measurable phenomena of the RP in a way that connects naturally with everything else we know about the neural basis of decision-making and strips away the conceptual basis for relating the RP to the timing of conscious awareness. Indeed, if the decision to move is marked by the time of **threshold crossing**, then awareness of conscious intention to move coincides with the decision point, as common sense would suggest.

The implications for this picture of volition for the free will debate are not entirely straightforward, as the details interact with substantive philosophical positions on free will. Stochastic models may yet pose problems for free will, but not because of the relative timing of awareness and volition. According to the AtBM, threshold crossings are partly the result of noise in the system that drives the decision variable over threshold. This suggests that noise is the source of an agent’s decision to move when they did, as opposed to at some other moment. **Agent-causation** theorists, who hold that freely willed action requires that the agent be uncaused to act but yet be the cause of its action, will likely look dimly on noise as an agential font of action \[[53](#R53)–[55](#R55)\]. Other theorists who want to identify the source of action as the agent will have to tell a story that somehow makes a case for the noisy trigger being part of or attributable to the agent \[[55](#R55)\]. As the AtBM incorporates a shift close to the threshold as a background for the determinative influence of noise, this shift can arguably be agentive or volitional.

**Incompatibilists** who hold that free will requires that our actions be undetermined may be happy with the AtBM, if the noise in the signal is indeterministic \[[56](#R56),[57](#R57)\]. Nothing in the model itself dictates whether or not that is the case and neuroscience is unlikely to definitively answer that question \[[58](#R58),[59](#R59)\]. Compatibilists can also be satisfied by this model, since determinism tends not to be an obstacle for them \[[14](#R14),[15](#R15),[60](#R60)–[63](#R63)\]. However, some **compatibilists** may be bothered by the decisions being precipitated by noise and not, one might argue, fully determined by the agent. These worries may be lessened in that many compatibilists will reject the standard Libet paradigm, in which an agent has no reason to choose to move at any particular moment, as a central case in which freedom of the will is at issue. Instead, they will be content to allow an agent to abdicate causal control to a subpersonal or nonpersonal mechanism in circumstances where no considerations bear on the outcome \[[14](#R14),[15](#R15),[64](#R64)\]. This contentment persists only if, in cases where one decides for reasons \[[65](#R65)\], it is the weight of the reasons and the agent’s weighing of those reasons that are determinative causal factors. A strength of SDMs is that they provide a unifying story that seamlessly allows agents to move between reason-driven and random decisions, as the spontaneous action case is just an SDM driven by noise in the absence of evidence/reasons.

Other versions of the SDM in which excursions to threshold are driven by noise and signal, whether motivational impulses or motor ideation, are even more congenial interpretations in which the agent is the source of threshold crossings. These signals have interpretations that can be linked to motivation or other agentive processes, making it easier to see the agent as the source of individual motor acts.

## Concluding Remarks

The RP continues to be both a methodological tool and an object of study, but there are significant areas about which we remain unsure, despite advances (see [Outstanding Questions](#BX6)). If recent models of the RP are on the right track, we cannot infer from the existence of the phenomenon that it reflects an actual signal in the brain that, in individual trials, has the characteristics of the RP, or that has causal efficacy. Because of this, one cannot infer that we lack conscious free will based on the temporal profile of the RP. If these models are correct, they may have implications for our understanding of free will, but none that avoid significant and substantive philosophical commitments. But given all the other reasons that have been raised for rejecting the classical interpretation (e.g. \[[3](#R3),[14](#R14),[16](#R16),[17](#R17)\]), even if SDMs are mistaken and the RP does reflect a real neural signal, albeit one difficult to detect on individual trials, the RP would still fail to support the classic inference for the inefficacy of conscious will.

### Outstanding Questions.

Why is there so much variability between subjects in the temporal profile and amplitude of the RP?

Why do some experimental subjects not exhibit a readiness potential at all?

What is the difference/connection between the RP, CNV, and SPN? Do they all share a similar set of neural processes? Is the difference between them a reflection of the differential recruitment of these processes due to slightly different task demands?

Does the readiness potential reflect initiation of action, or something more general such as anticipation or attention?

Which is correct: late- or early-decision models (or neither)?

What is the relationship between the RP and consciousness? Are the neural processes involved in generating the RP the same processes that lead to consciousness of intention?

Is there a discrete neural RP-like signal present on every trial, but just hidden in the noise? Or does it only exist in the average?

If there is a discrete neural signal that reflects the initiation of movement present on every trial or for every movement, what is its shape and its temporal relationship to movement onset?

If movement generated as a response to stimuli or to reasons is the result of an accumulation-to-bound process operating on evidence, then is self-generated movement just the same decision process, but in this case operating without external inputs in a stochastic milieu?

What brain activity is genuinely predictive of the onset of uncued movement?

## Highlights.

The readiness potential (RP) has been widely interpreted to indicate preparation for movement and is used to argue that our brains decide before we do. It thus has been a fulcrum for discussion about the neuroscience of free will.

Recent computational models provide an alternative framework for thinking about the significance of the RP, suggesting instead that the RP is a natural result of the operation of a stochastic accumulator process of decision-making, analyzed by time-locking to threshold-crossing events.

These models call for a reevaluation of: (i) the ontological standing of the RP as reflecting a real, causally efficacious signal in the brain; (ii) the meaningfulness of temporal comparisons between the ‘onset’ of the RP and the timing of other phenomena; (iii) the moment at which we, as experimenters, identify that a decision to act has been made; and (iv) the relevance of the RP for discussions of free will.

How Neuroscience Undermined the Classical Free Will Argument And Why It Still Fails to Decide the Issue

INTRODUCTION

Among the many ways scientific thinking has challenged human self-understanding, few are as dramatic or widely discussed as the suggestion that neuroscience might decisively show we do not possess free will. In popular science writing and in philosophical debate alike, it has become almost a matter of common knowledge that experiments by Benjamin Libet and his successors demonstrated that our brains decide to act long before we are aware of having decided, and therefore that conscious agency is an illusion—a post hoc rationalization of processes initiated entirely subpersonally. The argument reaches its strongest form when experimental measurements place the neural onset of action in the critical position: a brain signal begins preparing the body for movement several hundred milliseconds before the subject reports becoming consciously aware of any intention to move.

The classical anti-free-will argument built on these findings follows a straightforward and forceful syllogism that has shaped two decades of philosophical debate and countless public discussions. Its structure is this: (premise 1) neuroscience shows that the brain begins preparing voluntary movement hundreds of milliseconds before subjects are consciously aware of any intention to move—meaning the decision to act occurs unconsciously; (premise 2) if a decision is made by unconscious neural processes without conscious causation, then it is not freely willed by the agent; (conclusion 1) therefore, at least for spontaneous actions, no one has free will. Furthermore, (observation 2) this effect is ubiquitous in laboratory conditions and scales to the types of simple voluntary choices Libet studied; (conclusion 2) therefore we lack free will generally, or at least over the domain of everyday unforced actions.

Over the past forty years, this argument has enjoyed remarkable success in popularizing a skeptical view of agency. Books by prominent neuroscientists have declared free will "not even wrong" and urged readers to accept that they are "just a bunch of lucky atoms"; philosophers have written authoritative-sounding essays on how Libet showed we lack free will; countless articles, lectures, and podcasts have repeated the conclusion as settled science. Even defenders of free will often grant the empirical ground: many prominent libertarians and compatibilists alike accept that conscious awareness lags neural preparation by hundreds of milliseconds in simple motor tasks. The argument has, in this sense, been extraordinarily effective at establishing its conclusions—or so the debate appears on its surface.

Yet beneath this apparent consensus lies a structure that is far more fragile than most participants in the debate have recognized. When one examines the neuroscience itself carefully—as well as the philosophical premises that connect that neuroscience to grand metaphysical conclusions—the classical argument collapses on multiple fronts. The empirical measurements do not establish what they are taken to establish; the interpretation of the data remains genuinely contested among specialists, and plausible alternative models are at least as consistent with the evidence as the dominant interpretation. Even if one grants the empirical claims at face value, the philosophical inferences from those claims to sweeping skepticism about free will involve premises that are deeply contestable—and some of which, upon closer inspection, appear false. The argument may have seemed decisive in part because it was widely understood through a lens that made its conclusions follow almost trivially; but once that lens is removed or revised, the argument loses its momentum and persuasive power almost entirely.

This essay argues two interconnected claims. First, I argue that the classical free-will argument's empirical foundation—a smooth trajectory of increasingly decisive evidence against agency, culminating in fMRI prediction experiments—is misleading, because the key measurements remain deeply ambiguous, interpretively contested, and far less conclusive than the orthodox narrative suggests. Second—and equally important—I argue that even granting all the empirical claims that neuroscientists make about the timing of unconscious versus conscious decision processes, the philosophical bridge from those premises to the conclusion that we lack free will is extremely narrow and rests on assumptions that cannot be established without already settling the metaphysical debate in question.

THE CLASSICAL ARGUMENT STEP BY STEP

To evaluate the classical argument fairly, one must take its strongest form rather than a caricature. The argument's empirical core can be reconstructed through three landmark findings that appeared sequentially in the literature and each of which was taken to tighten the noose around libertarian agency.

The first and most famous finding comes from Libet's original experiments (Libet 1983, 1985). Subjects were asked simply to flex a finger at any moment they chose, while their EEG was recorded and their subjective timing of conscious intention was measured by reference to a rapidly rotating clock dial. The results showed that the readiness potential—a slow buildup of electrical potential over the motor cortex detectable in the average EEG trace—began approximately 500 milliseconds before movement onset. Meanwhile, subjects reported becoming consciously aware of their intention to move at approximately 200 milliseconds before movement onset. Because the RP onset preceded conscious awareness by roughly 300 milliseconds, Libet concluded that "cerebral initiation even of a spontaneous voluntary act … can and usually does begin unconsciously" (Libet 1985). For many readers, this result seemed decisive: if the brain prepares to move before you are aware of wanting to move, then your conscious self is not the cause of the action.

The second key finding came over a decade later, when fMRI studies by Soon, Freyschinger, Bosse, and Haynes (2008) appeared in *Nature Neuroscience*. Using multivoxel pattern analysis on 16 subjects making "free" choices between pressing a left or right button at an undetermined time, the researchers reported that activity differences in the precuneus and supplementary motor area predicted the subject's choice with above-chance accuracy up to ten seconds before the reported moment of conscious decision. The study's authors stated that "decision-related information" in these regions "remained unconscious for up to 10 s" (Soon et al. 2008). In popular and philosophical discourse, this finding was widely celebrated as a massive extension of Libet's timeline—not just hundreds of milliseconds but seconds of unconsciously decided action.

A third set of findings came from work attempting to measure the "point of no return" in self-initiated movement—the moment after which conscious intervention can no longer stop an impending action. Hay, Lau, and Roskies (2006) initially suggested that the point-of-no-return occurs 350 milliseconds before movement onset, a window larger than what Libet's data alone would allow and thus potentially leaving room for genuine "free won't" (i.e., a conscious veto power after Libet acknowledged it). But subsequent work from Hay et al. (2010) showed that the period of time between conscious awareness of intention and movement onset in Libet's task was approximately 350 ms—meaning there would only be about 350 milliseconds available for any such veto, a very narrow window indeed. Later studies further compressed this window: Rakwal and Pashler (2014) found no independent evidence for 'free won't' beyond what Libet himself had claimed, effectively undermining the retreat that many free-will defenders had sought in a post-decision veto mechanism. These findings combined to create an impression of ever-shrinking space for conscious agency—first hundreds of milliseconds of unconscious initiation, then increasingly narrow remaining windows for conscious control, and finally the effective elimination of all such residual room.

The classical argument now appears formidable, and its narrative is almost irresistible in its simplicity: the science steadily closed in on agency, first showing unconscious neural preparation starting well before awareness, then demonstrating that fMRI could detect those preparations seconds beforehand, and finally showing that even after awareness strikes, there is barely any time left for conscious intervention. By combining these empirical claims with the philosophical premise that an action initiated unconsciously is not freely willed, one arrives at a powerful case against free will.

THE EMPIRICAL CASE: WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY SHOW

Despite the popularity of this narrative, none of its empirical pillars supports the conclusions drawn from them as strongly as the orthodox account suggests. A closer examination reveals deep ambiguities, methodological limitations, and competing interpretations that the popular narrative systematically suppresses.

Consider first Libet's readiness potential findings. The RP is derived by averaging electroencephalogram traces time-locked to voluntary movement across many trials. The signal emerges only after averaging, at an amplitude order of magnitude weaker than background noise in individual trials (Roskies et al. 2021). This has led some researchers to question whether the RP exists as a discrete, identifiable signal on any individual trial or whether it is instead a statistical artifact—a consequence of how the data are processed rather than a reflection of a real neural event with an objective onset time in single-trial recordings (Roskies et al. 2021). The temporal profile of the RP has been described both as approximately linear and as nonlinear and exponential-looking, and its exact shape varies significantly across experimental conditions—including differences in task demand, movement effector, limb dominance, attention to timing, and even whether subjects hold libertarian or compatibilist philosophical beliefs (Roskies et al. 2021).

More importantly, the interpretation of the RP's onset as marking the beginning of "movement preparation" has been powerfully challenged by an alternative family of models: stochastic decision models (SDMs) (Schurger et al. 2012; Schurger 2021; Roskies et al. 2021). According to these models—which have substantial formal and empirical support—the RP in the movement-locked average does not reflect a gradual buildup toward a predetermined decision but rather the natural byproduct of ongoing stochastic fluctuations in neural activity, where the precise timing of movement onset is partly determined by whatever random fluctuation happens to cross a threshold at any given moment. In this "late-decision" interpretation, the RP's apparent early onset is an artifact of trial averaging coupled with selective sampling: because one only observes what happens on trials that culminate in movement, and because movement tends to occur when ongoing noise happens to push the decision variable over threshold, time-locking to movement onset is mathematically equivalent to time-locking to crests in a stochastic process. The RP's characteristic ramp shape emerges necessarily from this averaging procedure without any commitment to a genuine preparatory buildup beginning at some determinate point (Schurger et al. 2012; Roskies et al. 2021).

Under the late-decision interpretation, the subjectively reported time of conscious intention coincides with the actual neural event of threshold crossing—the decision point—just as common sense would suggest, rather than lagging far behind it (Roskies et al. 2021). This means that if SDMs are correct (and they are at least as consistent with the data as early-decision models), the apparent gap between conscious intention and neural preparation that drove Libet's skeptical inference shrinks dramatically or disappears entirely. The RP onset on this model is "physiologically meaningless: it does not mark a causally efficacious neural event or process" (Roskies et al. 2021). The classical argument loses its central empirical premise when this alternative interpretation—an interpretation that has become increasingly dominant among neuroscientists themselves—is taken seriously.

The fMRI prediction finding of Soon et al. (2008) suffers from equally serious limitations, even if one grants the result as reported. The study's accuracy was "statistically significantly above chance" but only "marginally better than a random guess" (Roskies et al. 2021; see also the original *Nature* publication). The prediction was made using information from large-scale brain regions in aggregate, not from identifiable discrete decision events, and the ten-second lead time is difficult to reconcile with known neurophysiological constraints on reaction times and neural processing speeds (Wittgenstein, Kahn, and Ramakrishnan 2023). Furthermore, because fMRI measures hemodynamic responses—a slow process relative to neural firing—the reported "prediction" might reflect not unconscious decision formation as such but more general states of arousal, preparation, or attentional bias that precede decisions and that cannot reliably distinguish between competing intentions until much closer to the moment of choice (Wittgenstein, Kahn, and Ramakrishnan 2023; Roskies et al. 2021). The claim that "decision-related information" is present in these regions ten seconds beforehand thus conflates correlation with causation in a way the data do not support, at least not as strongly as reported.

Even if one accepts all of Libet's and the fMRI findings at face value, the methodological limitations of the tasks themselves severely constrain their significance for free-will debates. Few philosophers have taken them far enough seriously, but it is well established that Libet-style tasks involve arbitrary decisions in which subjects "have no reason to choose to move at any particular moment" (Roskies et al. 2021; cf. Fischer 2017). This means the paradigm captures a very narrow and unrepresentative slice of decision-making. Most real-world decisions—those relevant to moral responsibility, practical deliberation, and the kind of agency that matters for free-will debates—are reason-responsive: they involve weighing considerations over extended periods and are not governed by moment-to-moment stochastic fluctuations in neural noise. The spontaneous-action case, which is just "an SDM driven by noise in the absence of evidence/reasons," represents a qualitatively different decision process from reason-driven deliberation (Roskies et al. 2021). Even libertarians who might be sympathetic to stochastic accounts can reasonably reject the Libet paradigm as capturing an edge case—one in which one has abdicated causal control to a subpersonal mechanism precisely because "no considerations bear on the outcome" (Roskies et al. 2021)—rather than the central paradigm for evaluating free will. This limitation does not refute the experimental data, but it severely constrains their philosophical inference: even if stochastic models correctly describe how the brain handles arbitrary, reasonless choices, that fact tells us nothing about how reason-responsive deliberation works or whether agents have control in cases where reasons genuinely determine decisions.

The shrinking-window narrative of "free won't" also faces serious challenges. If one accepts Hay et al. (2010) at face value, the window between W-time and movement is approximately 350 ms—narrow but not zero. Meanwhile, Rakwal and Pashler (2014) showed that evidence for any conscious veto beyond Libet's own claims is thin to nonexistent. But this finding itself is not decisive against libertarian freedom: compatibilists can argue that a genuine ability to act otherwise in a robust sense does not require milliseconds of control over reflexive motor mechanisms. The relevant locus of agency may be elsewhere—in the formation of intentions, dispositions, and character states that shape when stochastic fluctuations are interpreted as urges to act and whether they are subsequently endorsed or rejected.

THE PHILOSOPHICAL BRIDGE: WHY THE EMPIRICAL FINDINGS DO NOT SETTLE THE METAPHYSICS

Even if one were convinced that all the neuroscience of the readiness potential and preconscious neural activity accurately shows what Libet claimed, a further inferential gulf separates those empirical findings from conclusions about free will. The philosophical premises connecting the data to metaphysical claims are deeply contestable—and some are arguably false on closer inspection.

The classical argument's core inferential move is: unconscious initiation + temporal precedence of neural preparation = absence of conscious causal efficacy in action. This moves from a descriptive claim about timing to a normative/metaphysical claim about the conditions for free action without sufficient justification. Two questions resist the inference.

First, what does it mean, conceptually, for an agent's decision "to be made" by unconscious processes if those processes are themselves the agent's own brain and cognitive architecture? If the unconscious neural activity leading up to a decision is not caused by some external force but is rather the product—and expression—of the same person who subsequently becomes consciously aware of resolving to act, does this truly undermine agency? Many compatibilist philosophers have argued that what matters for free will is not that conscious awareness initiates every motor command in real time but that decisions ultimately track the agent's reasons, values, and dispositions. From this perspective, a late-conscious-apperception of an unconscious deliberative process is not an illusion of agency at all but a natural feature of how any complex information-processing system works. The unconscious brain does not decide *despite* the rational self; it decides *for* the rational self, building up commitment to one option over others through processes that only later become available to conscious reflection.

Second, and even more problematically for the classical argument, the inference from "the brain prepares for action before awareness" to "conscious will is causally efficacious"—and then in the reverse direction—presupposes precisely the metaphysical position one is supposed to be arguing for. The argument begs the question against compatibilism by assuming that only a libertarian picture of agency (where conscious awareness initiates or significantly contributes to action at or before the moment of decision) can satisfy the requirements of free will. But compatibilists have offered sophisticated accounts of how conscious reasoning, deliberation, and endorsement function causally in agentive behavior without requiring millisecond-level control over motor pathways (Fischer 2017). Libertarians who reject determinism altogether need not grant that Libet's paradigm targets any decision type they recognize as central to moral responsibility.

A third philosophical difficulty with the classical argument concerns its implicit conception of consciousness and causal efficacy itself. The argument takes for granted that if a process begins before conscious awareness, it must be outside the agent's control or authorship—and this assumption has been challenged. Roskies' work on the relevance of brain imaging to free will (2007) emphasized that the mere detection of subpersonal processes preceding conscious awareness does not settle whether those processes are properly attributable to the agent, and Schurger et al. have argued that even the RP's existence as a real signal is questionable enough to make any inference from its timing to questions about agency philosophically unwarranted (Schurger 2013; Schurger et al. 2012).

The implications of stochastic models for the free-will debate are, in fact, far more nuanced than anti-free-will popularizers have recognized. Under the accumulation-to-bound model, noise plays a role in determining when threshold crossing occurs—the precise moment of action—but this does not entail that actions lack agents entirely or that they are randomly caused by some force external to the person. Agent-causation theorists may find little comforting in "noise as an agential font of action," but compatibilists can accommodate stochastic triggers within a broader picture of reason-responsive deliberation (Roskies et al. 2021). Incompatibilists who require that actions be undetermined might even welcome the AtBM's implications, depending on whether the noise is genuinely indeterministic (Roskies et al. 2021). Other theorists may view motivational signals producing "subthreshold motor impulses at random times" as part of what makes an action attributable to a person after all (Roskies et al. 2021). In short, stochastic models "pose problems for free will, but not because of the relative timing of awareness and volition"—which was the classical argument's central selling point (Roskies et al. 2021). They complicate, rather than collapse, the debate.

Wittgenstein, Kahn, and Ramakrishnan (2023) summarize one productive philosophical reorientation: neuroscience can illuminate how decisions are implemented, but it does not have much to say about whether those implementations satisfy the normative and metaphysical conditions that constitute free will. The gap between mechanism and meaning has been systematically underestimated by those who claim that the former settles the latter.

EVEN IF THE DATA SUPPORTED ANTI-FREE-WILL CONCLUSIONS: WHAT WOULD FOLLOW?

Let us grant the most ambitious interpretation of the evidence: unconconscious brain states determine simple choices seconds before awareness, the RP is a real preparatory signal with a meaningful onset time, the veto window does not meaningfully exist beyond what Libet observed. What follows for free will?

Even under this generous charitable reading, the empirical data tell us very little. A vast literature in philosophy has noted that Libet-style tasks involve arbitrary, reasonless choices—a paradigmatic case of an agent abdicating causal control precisely because "no considerations bear on the outcome" (Roskies et al. 2021; Fischer 2017). The philosophical relevance of this finding to decisions in which agents deliberate over reasons, weigh values, and form intentions through conscious reflection is unclear at best. A theory that claims neuroscience proves I lack free will because I cannot consciously initiate a finger flexion for which I have no reason might be criticized for studying the wrong kind of decision altogether (Fischer 2017; Roskies 2012).

Moreover, the empirical data are entirely silent on whether there exists a metaphysical faculty—call it libertarian free will—that could ground moral responsibility in worlds with different causal structures. Even if our actual brain mechanics operate as the classical argument attributes, one cannot infer from that description alone that no kind of free will (perhaps in a non-natural or non-physically realized sense) is consistent with the facts of cognitive architecture. The argument's move from descriptive premises about neural timing to normative claims about metaphysical possibility and moral responsibility has always been one of its most philosophically weak points—a gap between the methodology of neuroscience and the domain of philosophical inquiry that researchers and popularizers alike have routinely underestimated or ignored.

CONCLUSION

The classical neuroscience-based argument against free will achieved an extraordinary degree of consensus in part because it was widely treated as self-evident: once one accepts the empirical claims about when unconscious neural preparation begins relative to conscious awareness, the skeptical conclusion seems inevitable—that our subjective sense of agency is an illusion and that we are "just a bunch of lucky atoms" (Dennett 2014). The argument felt decisive because its premises connected so neatly to its conclusion.

But I have argued here that the argument's perceived strength rests on three layers of misperception. First, the empirical data it relies upon are less conclusive than commonly presented: the readings potential remains ontologically ambiguous (Schurger et al. 2012; Roskies et al. 2021), its interpretation is genuinely contested within neuroscience itself (Roskies et al. 2021), and the fMRI prediction findings are statistically weak, hemodynamically noisy indicators that conflate correlation with causation (Wittgenstein, Kahn, and Ramakrishnan 2023; Roskies et al. 2021). Second, the philosophical bridge from temporal-precedence data to conclusions about agency is philosophologically unsound—it presupposes precisely the metaphysical position it attempts to establish, and it ignores serious compatibilist accounts of how conscious reasoning functions causally in agentive behavior (Fischer 2017; Roskies 2012). Third, even granting all empirical claims at their strongest interpretation, the paradigm studied is so narrow—reasonless, arbitrary decisions under experimental constraint—that its relevance to the domain of morally and practically significant deliberation is, at best, an open question (Roskies et al. 2021; Fischer 2017).

None of this proves that free will exists. But it does show that the most influential scientific argument against it—the one that achieved the broadest consensus among philosophers and the public alike—was not as strong, or as decisive, as its advocates believed. The classical argument's perceived force came from a kind of intellectual compulsion: once you accept its empirical premises and its implicit metaphysical assumptions, the skeptical conclusion follows nearly trivially. Remove those assumptions, correct the empirical misreadings, and the argument loses almost all its persuasive power.

Whether neuroscience can ever address questions of free will directly remains an open meta-philosophical question. But what neuroscience *has* shown us clearly enough—through findings about the readiness potential, preconscious decision-related activity, and stochastic models of movement initiation—is not that agents are illusions but that the gap between mechanism and meaning is far wider than popularizers of scientific skepticism have acknowledged (Wittgenstein, Kahn, and Ramakrishnan 2023). The argument against free will derived from neuroscience may have seemed decisive in part because it was widely understood through a lens that made its conclusions follow almost trivially. But once that lens is scrutinized, the classical case crumbles. This does not establish libertarian or even compatibilist free will—far from it—but it does mean that at least two hundred years of philosophical debate on free will must continue. The science has not ended the matter; it has merely changed its terms.
